statement: Three fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the product of the three numbers rolled is a multiple of 4?

choices.misconception: I worked out the probability that the product is not a multiple of 4, and gave that instead.
I thought the product is a multiple of 4 only when at least one die shows a 4, so I worked out 1 - (5/6)^3.
I counted the cases with at least two even dice, but forgot that a single 4 with two odd dice also works.
I only made sure the product is even, which needs just one even die, giving 1 - 1/8.

hints: Count the cases where the product fails to be a multiple of 4.
The product fails when all three dice are odd, or when exactly one die is even and that die shows 2 or 6. Find both probabilities, subtract from 1, then check by counting the successes directly.
All odd: 1/8. Exactly one die even and it shows 2 or 6: 3 x (1/3) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4. So the product fails with probability 3/8.

solutions.reliable: Work with the complement. The product is not a multiple of 4 when it has at most one factor of 2. That happens if all three dice are odd, with probability (1/2)^3 = 1/8, or if exactly one die shows 2 or 6 and the other two are odd, with probability 3 x (2/6) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/4. So the product fails with probability 1/8 + 1/4 = 3/8, and the answer is 1 - 3/8 = 5/8. Check directly: at least two even dice has probability 1/2, and exactly one even die that shows 4 has probability 3 x (1/6) x (1/2) x (1/2) = 1/8, giving 1/2 + 1/8 = 5/8 again. The transferable idea: when two methods agree you can trust the answer, and when they disagree the difference shows which case was missed.

whyOnTest: Probability with divisibility needs careful cases, and a second method by complement catches the single-4 case that a direct count tends to miss.
